parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what holds an electron inside the metal and what a single incoming photon must do to get it out to the surface.
Hint 2: Focus on the word minimum - what is the smallest photon energy that can just free an electron with no kinetic energy left over?
parts.proper_answer: The work function energy is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of the metal, corresponding to emission with zero kinetic energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the photoelectric effect**
Think of electrons bound inside the metal. A single photon gives all its energy $hf$ to one electron. Part of that energy is used to escape the metal.

Step 2: **Define the minimum escape energy**
The work function $\Phi$ is that escape cost. It is the energy needed to just free an electron from the surface, so: $$hf = \Phi + E_{MAX}$$ When $hf = \Phi$, the electron escapes with $E_{MAX} = 0$. That is why it is a minimum energy.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 10.1 and imagine extending the straight line back to where $E_{MAX} = 0$. What frequency value on the $f$-axis does this correspond to?
Hint 2: At that intercept the photon energy is just equal to the work function, so use $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ with your threshold frequency to find energy in J.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the threshold frequency from the graph**
You have $E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$, a straight line of gradient $h$. When $E_{MAX}=0$, $f = f_0 = \Phi/h$. Extrapolate the line in Fig. 10.1 back to the $f$-axis. It meets at: $$f_0 \approx 5.45 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$$

Step 2: **Calculate the work function**
At threshold, all the photon energy goes into escaping: $$\Phi = h f_0$$ $$\Phi = (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(5.45 \times 10^{14})$$ $$\Phi \approx 3.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$ Keep 2 s.f. to match the graph reading.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall how to change a very small energy in J into eV by dividing by the elementary charge, then compare your result with Table 10.1.
parts.proper_answer: $\Phi = 3.6 \times 10^{-19} / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \approx 2.3 \text{ eV}$, so the metal is potassium.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert J to eV and identify**
Divide by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J eV}^{-1}$: $$\Phi = \frac{3.6 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 2.26 \text{ eV}$$ This matches the 2.26 eV value for potassium in Table 10.1, so the metal is potassium.

parts.label: (c)(i)
key_concepts: frequency dependence of maximum kinetic energy
hints: Hint 1: Increasing intensity at fixed frequency changes the number of photons, not the energy carried by each individual photon.
parts.proper_answer: No change. Photon energy $hf$ is unchanged as frequency is unchanged, so $E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$ is unchanged.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why maximum kinetic energy stays the same**
Intensity up at the same frequency means more photons per second, but each photon still has energy $E = hf$. Since $f$ and $\Phi$ are fixed, $$E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$$ does not change. One common mistake is to think brighter light means more energetic electrons - it does not.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think one-photon to one-electron: if more photons arrive per second, what happens to the number of electrons released per second?
parts.proper_answer: Rate of emission increases because higher intensity means more incident photons per unit time, so more photoelectrons are emitted per unit time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why the rate increases**
Light intensity is power per unit area, proportional to photon arrival rate at fixed $f$. Each photon can free at most one electron. More photons per second means more successful emissions per second, so the photoelectric current increases.
